transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-08-20
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Mills (Redwood AE), Priya Kapoor (Redwood SE), Martin Hale (AegisCore CTO), Lina Torres (ML Eng Lead), Samir Patel (Infra), Rachel (SRE)

Summary:
Quick scoping for a 2-4 week POC focused on capacity sizing and autoscale: reserved GPU pool for baseline, burst strategy for peak, fallback to smaller quantized variant + hosted fallback, success criteria around p99 latency, throughput, and cost per 1M tokens. Agree on benchmark plan and timeline.

Topics:
- Current infra and traffic profile
- POC success criteria (latency, throughput, quality)
- Reserved GPUs vs shared burst and burst sizing
- Autoscale triggers, warm pool, cold start behavior
- Fallback policies and model variants (quantized, 8-bit, cpu fallback)
- Benchmarks, metrics to collect, and run schedule
- Next steps and owners

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'll kick off, this is Jordan from Redwood, and with me is Priya, our SE. How's everybody doing?
[00:07] Martin: Good, thanks. Sorry if there is a bit of background noise, we've got a standup running.
[00:11] Priya: No worries. Quick agenda — focus on POC scope: capacity sizing, autoscale, benchmarks, timelines. We'll capture success criteria so your infra team can sign off.
[00:20] Lina: Sounds good. We're mainly trying to validate that the inference can handle our peak user-facing traffic and not blow up our cost.
[00:26] Samir: Right, and we need to show our security and SRE folks the fallback behavior — if the dedicated GPUs are saturated what happens.
[00:33] Jordan: Exactly. To kick off — can you describe current traffic shape? concurrency, avg tokens per request, p95 spikes?
[00:40] Lina: Sure. Typical concurrency is 60 rps, heavy peaks to 240 rps for ~5-10 minutes during batch releases. Avg prompt length maybe 120 tokens, responses around 80 tokens, so roughly 200 tokens per request. But there are also longer analytic jobs — maybe 1% of calls go past 2k tokens.
[01:02] Martin: We care about latency under 300ms p99 for the main UI flows, anything above that users notice. Cost target is under $60 per 1M tokens if possible.
[01:13] Priya: Good constraints to work with. For the POC we usually split work into two phases: 1) baseline with reserved GPUs to get steady-state throughput and latency, then 2) burst strategy tests to validate autoscaler and fallback. How long do you want to run each phase?
[01:29] Lina: We have two dev sprints, so ideally keep the POC to 2-3 weeks. Baseline + one big load-run should be enough.
[01:36] Jordan: That aligns with standard POC. For capacity sizing, we need target concurrency and model choice. Are you planning to use open 7B or a larger 13B for quality?
[01:46] Lina: We tested a 13B variant; quality is better. But if 13B is too costly, we can accept 7B quantized if latency improves.
[01:55] Priya: Ok. For rough sizing: on A100s a 13B fp16 model does ~X tokens/sec per GPU under our infra; an 8-bit quantized 13B can cut memory and sometimes improve throughput for batching. For the POC we'll propose reserving 2 GPUs as baseline and provisioning a burst pool of 4 GPUs for peaks — that gets you both stable throughput and headroom for the 240 rps spikes.
[02:18] Samir: Can you break down that calc? How do you go from tokens/sec to concurrency?
[02:22] Priya: Sure. If avg 200 tokens per request and desired concurrency 240 rps during peak, that's 240 * 200 = 48k tokens/sec. If a single GPU delivers ~12k tokens/sec for your model/config (example number), you'd need 4 GPUs to keep latency targets. Baseline of 2 GPUs handles typical 60 rps (12k tokens/sec).
[02:43] Martin: The 12k number — is that measured or an estimate? We need actual runs for POC.
[02:47] Priya: It's an estimate, we'll run microbenchmarks in staging. We'll include both fp16 and 8-bit quantized runs and the same sequence length distribution you provided.
[02:56] Jordan: On autoscaling — we recommend a warm pool + fast-burst strategy. Warm pool keeps N reserved GPUs pre-initialized; burst autoscaler adds GPUs from a burst pool with pre-warmed images. Worst case cold starts should be under ~20s if the KV cache is empty, but we'll design the runs to avoid repeated cold starts.
[03:14] Rachel (SRE): If we have a warmed container but cold KV cache, what's the effective latency hit for the first requests?
[03:19] Priya: First few requests will pay the KV cache fill cost — maybe 50-150ms depending on seq len. For long tail sessions it's more. We'll capture KV miss metrics in benchmarks.
[03:28] Samir: And fallback — if burst pool is exhausted, what are options?
[03:31] Priya: Two strategies: 1) fallback to a smaller quantized variant on the same infra (lower memory but maintain functionality), or 2) route to hosted Redwood endpoints on different region/hardware as a degraded service. Both are supported; routing policies can be latency-first or cost-first.
[03:46] Jordan: In practice we often combine both: try quantized variant first, then hosted fallback for extreme overflow. We'll show failover timelines in the POC runbook.
[03:54] Lina: For quality we need to compare outputs between 13B fp16 and 13B 8-bit quantized — acceptable if rouge scores drop less than 3% on our evals.
[04:03] Priya: We'll include quality evals: a sample eval set you provide plus a synthetic set matching your UX prompts. We'll run n=500 evals per variant.
[04:12] Martin: Timeline question — when can we get numbers?
[04:15] Jordan: If we get your traffic profile and staging access this week, Priya can run initial microbenchmarks in 3 business days. Then a 2-hour night-time load-run can validate autoscale and burst the following week. So end-to-end two weeks for first pass.
[04:29] Samir: About security — we need audit logs, KMS integration, and SSO for the control plane.
[04:34] Jordan: Yes, Redwood Private supports KMS/HSM and SAML SSO. For the POC we'll provide limited access credentials and audit logs exported to your S3 bucket. We'll include SOC2 material in the security pack.
[04:47] Martin: Any deal-breakers you typically see?
[04:50] Priya: Cold start times and cost overruns. We mitigate by warm pools, small autoscale step sizes, and cost alerts. Also network egress in cross-region fallbacks can be a surprise.
[04:59] Jordan: Another practical item — batching. For user-facing low-latency flows we recommend small batch sizes and aggressive KV caching; for analytics we use larger batches. We'll configure adaptive batching in the POC to meet latency SLOs.
[05:12] Lina: Adaptive batching — is that automatic?
[05:14] Priya: It's tunable. The runtime adjusts based on queued requests, but you can pin batch size vs latency. We'll show you the tradeoffs in the benchmark report.
[05:22] Speaker 1: (inaudible)
[05:25] Jordan: Ok let's talk metrics to capture during runs — p50/p95/p99 latency, success rate, tokens/sec, GPU utilization, queue length, KV hit rate, cold start counts, and cost per 1M tokens. Anything to add?
[05:38] Rachel: Also memory pressure and OOMs, disk io on the local cache.
[05:41] Priya: Yes, GPU memory and swap alerts. We'll enable detailed profiling for one run.
[05:46] Samir: About model variants: we want ability to pin a variant for canary then auto-roll back if quality regressions are detected. Does Redwood support canary rollouts?
[05:55] Jordan: Yes — canary with traffic split, automatic rollback if evals fail or error rate spikes. We'll demo rollback in the POC.
[06:03] Lina: On cost, your earlier estimate of under $60 per 1M tokens — can you model expected spend for our baseline traffic?
[06:10] Priya: We'll produce a cost model: baseline 2 GPUs running 24/7 plus burst usage hours. We'll show per-day and monthly estimates and sensitivity to model size/quantization.
[06:19] Martin: For the POC SOW — include the test plan, success criteria, exact cohort for canary, and acceptance sign-off.
[06:26] Jordan: Will do. Success criteria we've captured so far: p99 latency < 300ms for UI flows, throughput to handle 240 rps peaks with degraded fallback under heavy load, no quality regression > 3% on evals, and overall cost estimate within your target. We'll write these in the SOW.
[06:42] Speaker 2: (mumbled)
[06:45] Priya: Quick note on orchestration — our autoscaler can do step scaling every X seconds; we recommend a warm buffer of 25% over expected baseline to avoid oscillation. For example, baseline 2 GPUs, warm buffer 1 GPU, burst pool 4 GPUs; autoscale step adds one GPU at a time with a short cooldown.
[07:05] Samir: What's the time to provision a new GPU from the burst pool?
[07:08] Priya: If the burst pool is warmed it is almost immediate for the container to accept traffic — sub 5 seconds; if the instance instance needs to boot from scratch it could be tens of seconds. We'll ensure burst pool is pre-warmed for the scheduled load run.
[07:21] Martin: Can we set a maximum cost cap on the POC so it won't exceed a dollar threshold?
[07:26] Jordan: Yes, we can set cost limits and a hard guardrail to stop scaling beyond a budget. We'll include that in the runbook.
[07:33] Lina: On metrics export — Grafana or prometheus integration?
[07:36] Priya: We'll push to your Prometheus endpoint and provide a sample Grafana dashboard.
[07:40] Rachel: Also need encrypted logs.
[07:42] Jordan: Logs can be encrypted at rest and we can ship to your encrypted S3.
[07:46] Martin: Any limitations on private networking? We have strict VPC peering rules.
[07:50] Priya: For POC we can run in a dedicated VPC and use peering or an IPsec tunnel. For Private deployments we support customer-managed networking.
[07:58] Speaker 3: (unknown)
[08:00] Jordan: Let's sketch an explicit POC timeline: Day 0-2 — access + traffic profile ingestion; Day 3-5 — microbenchmarks (fp16, 8-bit) and sizing; Day 6 — baseline deploy and sanity checks; Day 7-10 — scheduled load-run + failover tests; Day 11-14 — analysis, final report, and acceptance. That's two weeks roughly.
[08:23] Lina: That works. We might need extra time for security review but we'll try to keep to two weeks.
[08:29] Samir: Can you outline the specific benchmark runs you will carry out?
[08:32] Priya: Yes. 1) Microbench: single GPU token/sec for seq lengths [128, 512, 2048] both fp16 and 8-bit; 2) Concurrency sweep: increment concurrency to target peaks measuring p50/p95/p99; 3) Burst test: simulate sudden spike to 240 rps for 10 minutes and verify scaling and fallback; 4) Degraded fallback: force burst pool exhaustion and validate quantized variant and hosted fallback route; 5) Quality evals: 500 examples across variants.
[09:01] Martin: For the quality evals please include randomized seeds and keep the prompts identical.
[09:06] Priya: Yep. We'll version the prompts and store them in the run artifacts.
[09:09] Speaker 1: (brief crosstalk)
[09:12] Jordan: Regarding telemetry — we'll collect traces to map request path, and instrument the KV cache latency per request.
[09:18] Rachel: Do you support tracing headers to correlate across our services?
[09:21] Priya: Yes we propagate trace context.
[09:23] Samir: Any special infra prep on our side?
[09:25] Jordan: Provide a staging environment with sample traffic endpoint and SSO/KMS details, plus firewall rules for Redwood IPs. We'll send a checklist.
[09:33] Lina: For the SOW, include acceptance criteria and a simple sign-off template so our PM can stamp it.
[09:38] Jordan: Will do.
[09:40] Priya: A couple of gotchas we usually call out in the SOW: burst pool costs, egress when falling back cross-region, and quantization quality diffs. We'll make them explicit.
[09:50] Martin: Competitors question: we've also been talking to Scale and Replicate — how quickly can you get us these numbers?
[09:56] Jordan: We can get initial microbenchmarks in 3 business days with your staging access. That typically beats alternatives because of our runtime kernels and pre-configured benchmarking harness.
[10:06] Samir: Can you run an end-to-end cold start test? We want to know worst-case latency for a cold room start.
[10:11] Priya: Yes — we'll include cold-start tests in the burst scenario and record median cold-first request time and p99 cold-first time.
[10:18] Jordan: Ok let's capture acceptance criteria verbatim: p99 latency for UI flows < 300ms; ability to handle 240 rps spike with fallback that preserves functional output; quality regression < 3% on your evals; no OOMs during the run; and POC cost model within 15% of target.
[10:38] Lina: We also want a short decision rubric: close if p99 < 300ms and cost within threshold; otherwise iterate.
[10:44] Jordan: Great. I'll include the rubric.
[10:47] Martin: One more — for the fallback hosted option, will data be logged in Redwood? We need data residency assurances.
[10:53] Jordan: For the POC we can route fallback to a private-hosted Redwood endpoint in your region or ensure payloads are not logged by default. We'll include an explicit retention policy.
[11:05] Rachel: Ok. Are we missing anything on network egress?
[11:08] Priya: We'll quantify egress in the cost model and include a scenario where fallback is off to show delta.
[11:14] Speaker 2: (quiet)
[11:16] Jordan: Let's confirm owners and dates — Jordan sends SOW by 2026-08-22; Priya shares benchmark template by 2026-08-21; AegisCore provides sample traffic and staging access by 2026-08-25; schedule load-run week of 2026-09-01.
[11:31] Lina: Sounds good.
[11:33] Martin: ok thanks, appreciate the clarity.
[11:36] Jordan: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the doc and a calendar invite for the load-run.
[11:41] Priya: Thanks folks.
[11:43] (call ends)
